articles.title_orig: China warns UK against EU-style tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles
articles.title_zh: China warns UK against EU-style tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.content_orig:
An observer notes that the moment it goes live, it commodifies a sensitive topic that should never be exploited
A Chinese AI girl group has sparked intense online backlash after announcing that one of its virtual members was “pregnant” to explain her departure.
BABYQUEEN, a four-member, K-pop-style AI girl group managed in Liaoning province in northeastern China, formed in September and has around 1,100 followers.
On October 13, the group posted an announcement written from member Mity’s perspective. Saying she was “pregnant” and would pause all public activities, Mity asked fans to respect her privacy and her new life, without identifying the “father.”
The post went viral, attracting more than 78 million views on Weibo and igniting fierce debate over the boundaries of humanlike identities for digital personas.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.
The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
The Reuters news agency could not immediately confirm the visit. The Pentagon and Israel’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and there was no immediate indication of what they discussed.
President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza began.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

articles.title_orig: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.title_zh: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Police give update after Australian MP hit by car
As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.
Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures â backed by experts â have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.
He was briefed by federal police â whose counter-terror squad is helping state officers investigate â and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Witnesses saw the suspect do a U-turn before striking the MP and then reversing to ram her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said.
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese has been emotional when he has spoken about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
The alleged attack has left Australia reeling
Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.
In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs â and in some cases their children â have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.
Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.
Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.
"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.

Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's domestic spy agency Asio, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.
"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the federal police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.
Helen Haines at Parliament House in Canberra
In the wake of the attack, a range of MPs have described wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.
Women in politics are particularly scared, said Victorian state MP Georgie Purcell, who shares part of her electorate with Haines.
"Being a woman in politics changes the way you move through the world. We consider where we park our cars, the route we drive home, if we hold public events," she said in a statement.
"For many of us, the news... is our worst nightmare".
Coalition Senator James Paterson told News24: "I'd like to say that I was surprisedâ¦ but I'm not at all surprised."
There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and â if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed â one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.
"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums â that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un ‘proof of life’ photos released by North Korea after wild rumors dictator died from brain hemorrhage
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un ‘proof of life’ photos released by North Korea after wild rumors dictator died from brain hemorrhage
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has released a fresh batch of apparent “proof of life” photos showing Kim Jong Un inspecting shoes and women’s clothing — after wild rumors swept social media claiming the dictator had died from a brain hemorrhage.
The images, published by North Korean state media on Monday, show a seemingly animated Kim examining children’s footwear, gesturing toward officials and inspecting women’s coats at a garment and footwear exhibition.
The photos surfaced just hours after sensational claims circulated online that the 42-year-old leader had suffered a massive brain hemorrhage, fallen into a coma and died after being rushed to Beijing for emergency treatment.
North Korea’s official Korean Central News Agency reported that Kim toured the exhibition on Monday, although the photographs have not been independently authenticated and it remains unclear exactly when they were taken.
In one image, Kim bends forward to inspect a tiny pink shoe held by a young woman wearing a pale pink, double-breasted dress.
Another shows the North Korean strongman standing with his legs apart, his arms outstretched and his mouth open as he appears to speak emphatically with an official.
A third captures Kim reaching toward the sleeve of a rust-colored women’s coat displayed on a mannequin, while several aides trail behind him.
The apparent public appearance comes after Wanjun Xie, a US-based Chinese dissident associated with the China Democracy Party, posted a series of explosive allegations on X on Sunday.
Xie initially claimed that Kim had died and that China had dispatched 9,000 troops to Pyongyang amid fears of a succession crisis.
He subsequently alleged that a team of specialists from Beijing’s Peking Union Medical College Hospital had been sent to North Korea on Saturday to treat Kim following a severe cerebral hemorrhage.
According to Xie’s unsubstantiated account, the North Korean leader slipped into a coma before being transferred to Beijing, where doctors were unable to save him.
His body was then secretly returned to North Korea, Xie claimed.
NEW: Kim Jong Un on Monday "looked round the venue of the garment and footwear exhibition of the field of light industry," DPRK state media said. The photo-report came after rumors emerging on social media suggested he had died yesterday. https://t.co/rAZQMp2Uk6 pic.twitter.com/hmjRn06KX5
None of the allegations were accompanied by medical records, photographs, identifiable witnesses or other independently verifiable evidence.
The claims nevertheless gained traction across so cial media and were picked up by several international outlets, including The Sun, which characterized the story as unverified speculation.
The rumors also raised questions about whether Kim’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong , had taken control of the secretive regime.
The latest photographs, however, appear intended to dispel speculation about the North Korean leader’s fate, although Pyongyang has not explicitly addressed the death reports.
Kim’s health has long been a subject of international scrutiny.
On Sept. 30, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service told lawmakers that Kim weighed roughly 140 kilograms — about 309 pounds — and faced an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease because of his severe obesity.
Nevertheless, the spy agency said it had detected no significant signs of ill health , reportedly citing Kim’s ability to run up stairs during an inspection of a naval destroyer.
North Korean state media previously reported that Kim attended the inauguration of the National Defense Revolution Museum on Oct. 11, with an account of the ceremony published two days later.
That appearance preceded the alleged medical emergency and therefore could not refute claims that his condition had suddenly deteriorated.
Rumors circulate that Kim Jong-un has died, thwarting Kim Ju-ae's succession plans and potentially plunging North Korea into civil war. The Chinese Communist Party has reportedly dispatched 9,000 troops to Pyongyang to assist Kim Ju-ae in stabilizing her regime. In preparation…
It is said that On October 17, Peking Union Medical College Hospital dispatched a team of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular medical experts to North Korea to participate in the rescue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who was in critical condition.
It is rumored that recently,Kim Jong-un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and Supreme Leader of North Korea, suffered a severe cerebral hemorrhage and fell into a coma. Although a team of medical experts from Peking Union Medical College Hospital was dispatched to…
The latest death scare also echoes a notorious false alarm in 2020, when Ji Seong-ho, a North Korean defector who became a South Korean lawmaker , claimed he was 99% certain Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery.
Kim subsequently appeared in public, and Ji apologized for spreading the erroneous claim.
That six-year-old prediction resurfaced during the latest frenzy, with some online accounts presenting it as fresh evidence that the North Korean leader had died.
The Post has sought comment from the governments of North Korea and China as well as from Peking Union Medical College Hospital.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.
OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.
Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices.
Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI.
Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies , the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange.
"Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO."
The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy.
In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology.
While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

articles.title_orig: Priest in Ecuador Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
articles.title_zh: Priest in Ecuador Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online.
Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday.
Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head.
Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest.
On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil.
“We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads.
According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred.
Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported.
CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
articles.title_zh: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
articles.content_orig:
President at Kansas rally tries to turn protests into cautionary tale for US as Republicans face midterm losses
Explainer: why are people protesting across Europe?
As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France ,” he said.
Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris .
“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”
The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally , whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar politcal opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hard-line immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day..
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.
Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, vice-president JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe , in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.
Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania , where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s close familyson-in-law, Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title_zh: Meet the researchers leaving the US because of Trump's funding cuts and politicization of science

Halley Froehlich never expected to leave the United States, where her family lineage stretches back to the 1700s, to pursue her scientific career.
Yet, faced with stalled federal grants and growing uncertainty over the country's research environment, she packed her life into boxes and relocated to Finland alongside her husband and daughter. She now studies how climate change affects edible fish, shellfish, and seaweed at the University of Helsinki .
Her departure reflects a wider trend. When the Trump administration began reshaping the American scientific sector last year by altering the federal grant distribution process and seeking greater political influence over funded projects, foreign academic institutions recognized an opportunity.
Many introduced dedicated schemes designed to entice U.S.-based scholars by offering stable financial support and academic freedom.
A growing number of academics have accepted these international offers. Though comprehensive nationwide data remains difficult to aggregate, university officials, researchers, and professional associations describe the ongoing shift as clear, unprecedented, and concerning.
"You can almost talk to any vice president for research at a university and they will tell you of one or two top faculty that they’ve lost," said Tobin Smith, senior vice president of government relations and public policy for the Association of American Universities.
White House spokesperson Liz Huston said Trump is "ending waste" and is "committed to keeping America the world leader in scientific innovation, and that means funding real science."
Despite those assurances, an April report from the Business for Federal Research Funding Coalition revealed that more than half of U.S. states have lost scientists to recruitment programs in other countries.
Survey data from last March indicated that early-career biomedical scientists were about 20 percentage points less likely to say they wanted to stay in the U.S. "now" than they did six months earlier.
Furthermore, figures from the American Institute of Physics show that physics Ph.D. graduates in 2025 departed the U.S. at the highest rate observed in 30 years.
Institutions in nations such as Canada , France , Belgium , and Finland are publicly advertising their success in drawing scholars from U.S. organizations. For a country that far and away leads the world in Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, and chemistry, researchers view this as a disturbing and surprising development.
"It used to be the shining city on the hill where we all want to go," said Christine Stawitz, now at the University of Birmingham in England . "That reputational loss, I think, is hard to quantify, but also really damaging."
Stawitz stepped down from her job at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last year to become a research software engineer in the United Kingdom .
She noted that NOAA no longer aligned with her values, particularly after receiving directives to strip websites of references to climate change and diversity, equity and inclusion topics.
She added that the state of American science has become a recurring topic of conversation at international gatherings. " People talk about the U.S. at conferences in the U.K. now like, I don't know what's going on there. It's not good," she said.
For Froehlich, the choice to relocate developed over time. Already concerned by issues surrounding school safety and gun violence in the U.S., she watched as the national research landscape was overturned.
At the University of California, Santa Barbara, grant postponements and cancellations left colleagues struggling and student researchers in tears. Doubts regarding future federal backing for her climate-focused research mounted.
"The cumulative effect of those things ultimately ended up making us really serious about, I don’t think here is our home anymore," said Froehlich.
She ultimately accepted an offer through an initiative by the Research Council of Finland, securing five years of guaranteed funding totaling about $3 million. She moved into a flat by the Baltic Sea in Helsinki and is taking university-sponsored Finnish lessons.
Foreign researchers who were drawn to the U.S. for its reputation as a global leader in science are also seeking different places to do their work.
Married biologists James Letts, who is Canadian, and Maria Maldonado, who is Argentinian, left their academic positions at the University of California, Davis to join Australia 's Monash University. Both earned their doctoral degrees in New York and spent over a decade doing science in the U.S.
Grant-related uncertainty—including laying off a staff scientist while waiting for stalled funding—motivated them to make the move.
"All I want to do is do great science and make discoveries, but I want my work to mean something as well. And the opportunity to do that seemed very difficult in the U.S.," Letts said.
Immigrants have historically won 40 percent of the U.S. science Nobel Prizes. However, Omar Yaghi, a 2025 Nobel Prize winner for chemistry, departed his position at the University of California, Berkeley this year to direct an artificial intelligence lab at China’s Tsinghua University.
The U.S. remains a science powerhouse, full of institutions with robust research communities and well-resourced facilities that attract foreign talent.
Even if every European country threw open its doors, there still would not be enough capacity to accommodate every American scientist. Many researchers are choosing to stay, searching for new sources of funding or pivoting to industry positions.
Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the ongoing erosion of reputation and talent. The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $174 billion in federal grants since the president's second term began, according to tracking data compiled by the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness.
Additionally, a proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget could accord political appointees more control over which future projects are funded, though a resolution approved by Congress has delayed a final decision on the rule until December.
Scientists who have moved away and those remaining in the U.S. are worried about what lies ahead. They warn that the next generation of scientists may face fewer graduate programs, diminished funding, and reduced mentorship—effects that could take a decade or longer for the U.S. scientific enterprise to fully feel.
Major research institutions accepted 15% fewer applicants for fall 2026 doctoral programs compared to last year, according to admissions data collected by the Association of American Universities. One of the impacted students was a mentee of Smith's.
"What is one of my pieces of advice to that young man? Next year, look in Canada," he said.

articles.title_orig: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.title_zh: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.content_orig:
Megan Harmes was 14 when she first tried ketamine.
A decade later, rehab is helping her rebuild her life after bladder issues caused by the drug have left her needing to wear incontinence pads.
The drugs charity Kaleidoscope says it has seen a huge rise in referrals to its detox and rehabilitation facility over the last five years, with two people referred in 2021 compared to 112 so far this year. The majority of clients are aged 18 to 24.
Research is now underway by the University of South Wales into the specific needs of this group, as the harm caused by "chronic, escalating use" of ketamine is far more rapid, over a shorter space of time, than from alcohol or Class A drugs.
Services traditionally designed for older adults are having to adapt to support much younger people, it said, with very different needs, with habits often formed while they were in school.
For 24-year-old Megan, from Flint in north Wales, drug use became more common among her peers during lockdown.
As an aeronautical engineering apprentice, she was suddenly working from home, on full pay, with access to a drug whose price had plummeted.
She said at its worst, she was on it "all day, every day", as according to Megan it helped to suppress symptoms or feelings associated with ADHD and borderline personality disorder.
"I'm very hyperactive now that I'm sober. I haven't been like that since I was 14, it suppressed pretty much everything," she said.
Eventually her ketamine use meant she lost her apprenticeship, causing her to "spiral".
Megan later found work elsewhere, but four years of night shifts further entrenched her use, as she would use ketamine to stay awake through the night even on days off.
For the last two years she has been in agony, unable to stand straight and needing to wear incontinence pads.
"For a 22-year-old wearing pads or nappies, it takes away all dignity," she said.
"Back then I really didn't care whether I lived or died - now I don't want to die.
"I've been in rehab just over four weeks and I'm getting back to my old self."
Megan said she wouldn't know the extent of the damage to her bladder for some time, but she has put on weight and is physically feeling better than when she arrived.
Jo Moore runs the Birchwood rehabilitation facility for Kaleidoscope and said five years ago they had just one referral for inpatient detox from ketamine.
"Since January this year we've seen 112 people come through the door," she said, adding that half their clients are currently being supported for ketamine use.
"It's very, very cheap and very accessible - that's what allows people to use it more frequently and at large amounts at the same time."
The drug is prescribed in healthcare settings as a dissociative anaesthetic, and also used with animals, but was reclassified as a Class B drug in 2014. This means it is illegal to take, carry, make or sell.
Illicit ketamine use among those aged between 16 and 59 in the UK was estimated to be about 264,000 people in 2024-25, with those seeking treatment for ketamine use disorders increasing twelvefold over the course of a decade.
While younger people have driven the rise in its use, Moore said the last year had seen a rise in referrals for adults aged 25 to 34, particularly in Cardiff and south-east Wales.
Dr Darren Quelch, from the University of South Wales, said interviews with service users at Birchwood suggested use started from as young as 13.
He said the physical harm caused by persistent use ranged from memory problems and chronic pain to bladder damage and kidney failure, but that support services were having to rapidly adapt as the needs of users are more complex.
"Their bread and butter isn't dealing with really complex medical presentations," he said. "Even if they were, we actually don't know what the right answer is yet."
He is now conducting research alongside Kaleidoscope to establish what types of support work for this specific patient group.
"The population is inherently different to lots of other groups that might engage with drug and alcohol treatment services," he said.
Mark said his health had deteriorated to such an extent that "at the age of 25 I probably had the body of an 80-year-old".
"I was no longer functioning like a proper human being," he said.
As a keen footballer growing up in Liverpool, he now looks on jealously at others his age, walking without pain.
"It stopped me being a father to the little girl that I've got - I stopped being the big brother, the responsible son," he said.
Mark would regularly pass clots and experience pain during urination, but said the collapse of his nose from snorting drugs has had a huge impact.
"It completely destroys self-confidence - which leads to more drugs, because that just blanked out what I think of myself."
It's one of the reasons he has asked to remain anonymous.
"I started getting looks of disgust from my own family, which destroyed me. It was a very lonely time through my addiction," he said.
Mark's drug use started at 18, but by 21 he said he was using "copious amounts of cocaine and ketamine".
He initially sought help from his GP in Liverpool, but was too ashamed to admit he was using ketamine for fear of being dismissed or judged.
"It's a hard lesson learned," he said.
It's an issue reflected in Quelch's research. He found young people struggled with A&E and GP surgeries, as their symptoms weren't always linked with ketamine use, or the question wasn't always asked.
"That's not necessarily because people aren't asking the right question, but we don't actually know what works well at the moment," he said.
"There's very little provision for young people experiencing drug and alcohol-related harms, and that has almost left us starting right from the beginning."
Moore said things were improving, with greater availability of early intervention in the community, reducing the need for detox.
"We're seeing less people presenting to services with a new substance use of ketamine - so the education in schools, colleges and universities is actually working.
"But we are seeing an increase in people that have been using for a couple of years that we are going to continue to have to help and support."
With trends in drug use evolving, Moore said the challenge for both the third sector and the NHS was to adapt around the needs of clients, but that the involvement of those with lived experience had made a difference.
"I can see improvements now, but there have been some really difficult times where it felt like we were shouting in the dark."
Quelch said while research continued, the scale of the current ketamine problem was still unclear, as was the longer-term health implications.
"Anecdotally, relapse is a big problem in this group - we don't know the recoverability of their bodies, but we have seen that when people resume using ketamine after a period of abstinence, those harms appear a lot quicker than the first time around," he said.
However, Quelch added the work being done with peer support at Kaleidoscope was "really unique and impactful".
"There was a lack of judgement or stigmatisation - the peer element was really important and is something to learn from the Birchwood environment."
For Mark it has meant a focus on the future is possible. Like many we spoke to, he was adamant he wanted to give something back.
"I grew up thinking money was everything, but I get joy now from helping other people who are struggling. I was there once and I know how much it means to get someone to help you."

French bonds and Paris-listed ‌stocks also fell as the widespread protests across France underscored the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit.
France's central government asked some local authorities to ‌impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday, after looting stemming from the protests.
Tech stocks on Wall Street recovered some ground after a bruising week, with an index of semiconductors up 1.6%. On Friday, the index ​sank in its eighth straight day of declines, its longest losing streak since 2008.
With results due from Meta on Wednesday, and results from Tesla and chipmakers Lam Research and Texas Instruments also due this week, investors will be watching for signs that massive AI spending ultimately pays off.
"Investors are buying the correction dip that we had," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York.
"The market is now going to go through a very critical test over the next two weeks. We have some big-name earnings coming out," he said. "In terms of technology, the test ‌of whether or not the spending on AI... will be met ⁠with satisfaction is going to be critical."

Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
After a bruising week for the tech trade, investors seem to have came back into the sector, with the Nasdaq Composite rallying overnight.
The optimism is cautious, with debt concerns still a key worry for a sector that has seen record bond issuance this year.
Investors are once again piling into tech, after fears over AI financing, rising competition and possible excess chip supply in a few years drove them to cash out of the market last week.
The Nasdaq Composite rebounded more than 1% on Monday, after sliding 4.5% last week and snapping a four-week winning streak.
Intel advanced 2% after JPMorgan analysts upgraded their rating on the chipmaker. Advanced Micro Devices added 1.8%, and Micron Technology jumped about 3%.
It was not a wholesale embrace of the sector, however. Funding concerns still loom, especially over neocloud companies.
Shares of neocloud mainstay CoreWeave reversed course from earlier gains, falling 0.4%, even after receiving Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to buy from neutral.
CoreWeave shares plunged more than 25% last week — their biggest one-week drop since November 2025 — over debt concerns.
Another company that is also facing credit stress is Oracle . It risks a credit rating downgrade that could tip its debt into junk territory. Oracle's rating at S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum.
While the bonds are still investment grade, the shift in sentiment can be seen in the spread of Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default.
Oracle's five-year CDS spread, or premium, is currently at 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 basis points on Thursday. It is up 287% in one year.
The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
When the year started, investors were predicting a slew of AI companies going public , including SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI.
But now investors will have to settle for less , with OpenAI ruling out its market debut in 2026 and several other planned offerings postponed this year .
On prediction market platform Kalshi , speculators think the only major company left that might officially announce an IPO this year is Anthropic, which confidentially filed a prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in early June.
Only Anthropic offers greater than 50% odds — 75% as of Monday morning — to officially announce an IPO this year, out of the 23 companies that Kalshi lists on its market that remain open to trade.
On the geopolitical front, the tensions between Washington and Kyiv continue to rise with President Donald Trump saying Monday he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss how to end the Ukraine war.
That comes after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump had floated the idea of a trilateral summit with Xi next month, although the meeting is envisioned to exclude Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump told reporters when asked about the potential meeting as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.
Trump also doubled down on his criticism of the Ukrainian leader when he was asked about Zelenskyy's remarks that Trump is on the wrong side of history , saying that "Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," and reiterating his call for Kyiv to "get a new president."

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.
That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.

Demonstrations over poor public services and rising costs spiralled over the weekend, with shops looted and property vandalised
Why are people protesting across Europe?
Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days ⁠of unrest that saw demonstrators ⁠clash with police, ​loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.
The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at ⁠a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.
“From words to action: 500 more ⁠troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.
Most stores in Milan’s Via ​Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior, had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.
Several hundred hooded ‌protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.
Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who ‌faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.
“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.
As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.
Italian ⁠police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of ​those taken to police stations, 32 were ​arrested, including 23 minors and 13 ​foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

articles.title_orig: Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese
articles.title_zh: Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese
articles.content_orig:
Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the Temporary Protected Status policy will be able to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation for the time being, even though their protections were set to expire soon, the Department of Homeland Security told CBS News on Sunday.
The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.
But in statements on Sunday, DHS said final decisions on the fate of the humanitarian immigration programs will "be made at the appropriate time."
Until such decisions are announced, DHS added, nationals of Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the TPS program will "retain protection."
The decisions to keep the deportation protections in place, albeit not final, stand in sharp contrast to the Trump administration's broader posture toward TPS programs.
Trump administration officials have routinely denounced TPS as a de facto amnesty policy abused by the Biden administration that encourages illegal immigration and that has been extended too often, despite its temporary nature.
Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration, as part of its aggressive immigration crackdown, has revoked the TPS protections of more than 1 million immigrants from over a dozen countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.
The programs for Ukrainian and Sudanese nationals are among a handful of TPS policies that have remained in place nearly two years into President Trump's second term, alongside the protections for tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador. Their TPS program was also set to lapse last month, but DHS retained their protections, pending a final announcement.
Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows the U.S. government to offer a temporary deportation reprieve and work permits to immigrants, illegal and legal alike, who hail from countries facing armed conflict, an environmental disaster or another crisis that makes their return there unsafe.
The TPS policy for Ukrainians was first announced by the Biden administration in the spring of 2022, soon after Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine. As of March 2025 , there were more than 100,000 Ukrainians enrolled in TPS, including those allowed into the U.S. under a Biden-era sponsorship policy.
The TPS program for Sudan has been around since the late 1990s, with different administrations extending the policy due to the armed conflict and political turmoil that has plagued the African nation. As of March 2025 , roughly 1,800 Sudanese nationals had TPS.
This story published first on CBS News at 1:44 p.m. on Oct. 18, 2026.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."
"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18 .
But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:
"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."
Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.
Read more: How much does a millionaire actually owe the IRS on tax day?
"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.
Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce ( CRM ), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."
Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.
Read more: 10 ways the One Big Beautiful Bill Act affects student loans and financial aid
As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.
There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.

A dip in the jet stream will also funnel in moisture from the Pacific as a strong low-pressure system moves into the region.
Wednesday: The highest risk of flooding on Wednesday covers much of Arizona and parts of New Mexico, as well as southern portions of Colorado and Utah.
There will be an abundance of moisture available to support heavy downpours and training storms. This means storms will produce heavy rain over the same areas for long periods of time. The Weather Prediction Center is forecasting rainfall rates as high as 2 inches per hour.
Some of the biggest concern will be the possibility of mudslides over recent burn scar areas as well as slow canyons and arroyos.
If you have plans to visit any of the national parks in the West this week, make sure you check the forecast daily and pay attention to any warnings or advisories issued.

Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.
The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised.
In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped .
Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".
Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."
The new rules will give drivers:
Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.
Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.
With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.
The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.
The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.
The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.
But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament.
The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice".
The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.
Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".
But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.
The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

articles.title_zh: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
articles.content_orig:
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt , and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble . Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “ How are we planning on affording this, champs? ”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it , that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic , co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings , owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans , and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while . As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds , too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.
Anyway, some people are buying the dip .

articles.title_zh: GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide. See affected products
articles.content_orig:
How to Live Better, Longer
Federal inspectors who spent six days inside a Houston compounding pharmacy in August documented 14 problems with how it made sterile injectable drugs, including compounded GLP-1 weight-loss shots , according to an FDA inspection report . The pharmacy, Houston RX LLC, later recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide with niacinamide because of a lack of assurance of sterility.
The findings matter to anyone who buys compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide through a telehealth program, clinic, or med spa. Injectable drugs bypass the skin's natural barrier, so a contaminated vial can cause infection at the injection site or, less often, in the bloodstream. Patients usually cannot tell a safe vial from a compromised one by looking at it. Equipment that has not been depyrogenated, a process that removes fever-causing bacterial residues called endotoxins, can leave those residues behind even when no live germs remain.
The report, known as a Form 483, lists observations made during an inspection. The document states that these observations do not represent a final FDA determination about compliance, and the company can respond or correct them. MedicalDaily could not locate a public response from Houston RX.
Investigators inspected the pharmacy on Vantage Parkway East on six days between August 20 and August 28 and issued the report on the final day. The first observation is blunt: "Personnel performed aseptic manipulations with exposed hair or skin." Inspectors wrote that an operator working inside the ISO 5 hood, the cleanest workspace, had exposed skin on her forehead while stoppering freshly filled semaglutide-niacinamide vials.
Other observations describe the cleanroom air. Pressure readings from July 10 to August 21 between the buffer room and the less clean anteroom were all negative, a reversal that can let dirtier air drift toward sterile work. The report says lots made during that period were released.
Inspectors also wrote that on August 3 the pharmacy recovered microbial growth in the ISO 5 hood after filling a lot of tirzepatide-niacinamide. No investigation followed because the firm's action level was not appropriate, according to the FDA, and that lot was released and partially distributed.
The report adds that staff pressed stoppers into vials by hand, that vials were finished outside the clean area, and that beakers, stir bars and graduated cylinders used for sterile drugs were not sterilized or depyrogenated. A ceiling vent just outside the cleanroom had water stains and what appeared to be mold. On one inspection day, it was dripping condensate near the area where items headed into the cleanroom were wiped down.
Ingredients were another concern. Certificates for the tirzepatide and semaglutide active ingredients were marked for research and development only, as were certificates for other ingredients, and a sermorelin ingredient was labeled for scientific research use. The niacinamide used in all of the pharmacy's GLP-1 formulas met a dietary supplement standard rather than a pharmaceutical one, and several ingredients were not stored at their labeled temperatures.
According to FDA enforcement records summarized in the nonprofit MedShadow Foundation's roundup of recent compounded GLP-1 drug recalls , Houston RX began recalling 64 two-milliliter vials of tirzepatide-niacinamide 20 mg/2 mg per mL on September 25. The FDA classified it as a Class II recall, meaning use may cause temporary or medically reversible health problems, or that serious harm is unlikely. The pharmacy also recalled seven vials of compounded sermorelin, a growth hormone-releasing peptide, citing a lack of process control.
Recall details are posted in the FDA's weekly Enforcement Report database . Patients who use compounded tirzepatide should check the pharmacy name on the label or ask the prescriber which pharmacy filled the order.
Signs of a possible injection-site infection include spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus or pain that gets worse. Fever, chills, a racing heart, or confusion after an injection can signal a more serious infection and need urgent care. Patients should not stop a prescribed treatment without talking with a clinician, but they can ask for a replacement from a different source.
Side effects and product concerns can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program , and patients can keep the vial and packaging until they speak with a pharmacist.
Cost drives much of the demand. An October price survey by NexLife, a telehealth company that sells compounded GLP-1s, found a median all-in price of $222 a month for compounded tirzepatide across 14 online programs and $175 for compounded semaglutide across 16, according to its release on GlobeNewswire . Those figures were compiled by the company and have not been independently verified.
The trade-off is oversight. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and the agency's page on unapproved GLP-1 drugs reports 990 adverse event reports tied to compounded semaglutide and more than 730 tied to compounded tirzepatide as of May 31, 2026. The FDA says adverse events from compounded versions are likely underreported, though the reports alone do not prove the drugs caused the problems.
Houston RX is not the only pharmacy with recent sterility-related recalls. The same MedShadow roundup lists recalls of compounded GLP-1 products by Carolina Infusion in Ridgeland, South Carolina, and Apothecary Pharma in Cary, North Carolina.
Patients using compounded products can ask whether the pharmacy is licensed in their state, whether it has recent FDA inspection findings, and whether an FDA-approved version is covered by their insurance. Any further FDA action, such as a warning letter, would depend on the agency's review. For now, the recall notice and inspection report are the clearest public record of what inspectors found.
What did the FDA find at Houston RX?
An August inspection produced a Form 483 listing 14 observations, including exposed skin during sterile work, reversed cleanroom air pressure, microbial growth in a clean hood, unsterilized equipment, possible mold near the cleanroom, and research-grade ingredients.
Which products were recalled?
Houston RX recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide 20 mg/2 mg per mL due to a lack of assurance of sterility and seven vials of compounded sermorelin due to a lack of process control. Both are Class II recalls.
How can I tell if my vial is affected?
Check the pharmacy name on the label and compare it with the FDA Enforcement Report. If you are unsure, ask your prescriber or the dispensing pharmacy.
No illnesses linked to the recalled vials have been publicly reported. The FDA has received more than 1,700 adverse event reports involving compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide overall, but those reports do not establish cause.
What symptoms should I watch for after an injection?
Watch for spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or worsening pain at the injection site. Fever, chills, a fast heartbeat, or confusion need urgent medical care.
Should I stop my GLP-1 treatment?
Do not stop a prescribed medication on your own. Contact your prescriber to discuss a replacement from another pharmacy or an FDA-approved option.
